exec.plain: Executive communication is how you talk to senior customer leaders, such as a CIO (Chief Information Officer, the person responsible for a company's technology), when the stakes are high. Executives have little time and care about outcomes: money, risk, customers and deadlines. Good executive communication means giving the answer first, translating technical numbers into business effects, and asking for one clear decision. It also covers calming an escalation, which is when an unhappy customer takes a problem over your head to someone more senior.
exec.analogy: Think of a hospital doctor talking to a worried family. The surgeon does the technical work, but the family needs a short, honest update: how the patient is, what happens next, and when they will hear again. Nobody wants a lecture on suturing technique while they are scared.
exec.why: FDEs sit inside the customer, so when something breaks, the executive often hears about it before your own company does. Picture an insurer's claims assistant slowing down on a Tuesday morning and the CIO emailing your sponsor that it is 'completely broken' and the renewal is in doubt. How you handle the next few hours, technically and in writing, decides whether the account grows or shrinks.

subtopics.title: Two tracks during an incident
subtopics.body:
An incident is any event where the system stops doing what users need. During an incident you run two tracks in parallel. Track one is technical: find the cause and restore service. Track two is human: keep the people affected informed and calm.

New FDEs often drop track two because the technical problem feels more urgent. The result is silence, and silence makes executives assume the worst. A short message every hour or so, even when nothing has changed, keeps trust intact while you debug.

If your pod has two people available, split the tracks between them. One person debugs. The other writes updates, fields calls and keeps a timeline. When you are alone, set a timer so you remember to send updates.
subtopics.example: An insurer's claims assistant slows from 2 seconds to 8 seconds per answer at 10:00. You post a holding note to the CIO at 10:20, start pulling logs, and find at 11:05 that a vendor API is rate limiting your calls (refusing requests because you sent too many). You switch to cached results as a workaround at 13:40. Between 10:20 and 13:40 the CIO received three short updates, so the escalation never grew.
subtopics.code:
INCIDENT TIMELINE  (keep this open in a shared doc)
time   track   entry
10:00  tech    p95 latency alert fires: 8.1s (normal 2s)
10:20  people  Holding note to CIO + sponsor. Next update 11:30.
10:45  tech    Scope: all regions, started 09:58, no deploy today
11:05  tech    Logs show HTTP 429 from policy-lookup vendor API
11:30  people  Update 2: cause found, workaround in progress, ETA 14:00
13:40  tech    Cached policy lookups enabled, p95 back to 1.3s
13:50  people  Update 3: resolved, full write-up by Wed 12:00
# Rule: every 'people' entry states the next update time.

subtopics.title: Listen and restate before you explain
subtopics.body:
Active listening means showing the other person you understood them before you respond. The simplest technique is to restate their problem in their own business terms: 'So the claims team is falling behind and customers are waiting longer for answers. That is the priority.'

Restating does two things. It lowers the emotional temperature, because the executive feels heard. It also checks that you are solving the right problem. Sometimes the executive's real worry turns out to be a board meeting on Thursday, which changes what you should prioritise.

After restating, say three things: what you are doing now, when they will hear from you next, and who to call in the meantime. Avoid technical explanations at this stage. You do not know the cause yet, and guessing out loud creates promises you may have to take back.
subtopics.example: A hospital's COO calls because nurses cannot see tomorrow's shift schedule in the new AI scheduling tool. You say: 'Nurses on three wards cannot see tomorrow's shifts, and that risks gaps in cover tonight. I am looking at it now with our engineer, and I will call you back by 15:00 with either a fix or a manual fallback.' You have not explained anything technical, and the COO knows exactly what happens next.
subtopics.code:
Subject: Scheduling tool - looking at it now

Hi Priya,

Thank you for flagging this quickly. My understanding: nurses on
Wards 4, 7 and 9 cannot see tomorrow's shifts, which risks gaps
in cover tonight.

What we are doing now: checking the data sync from your rostering
system, which is the most likely source.
Next update: by 15:00 today, with a fix or a manual fallback.
If urgent before then: call me on 07700 900123.

Sam (FDE)

subtopics.title: Translate metrics into business outcomes
subtopics.body:
Engineers measure things like latency (how long a request takes), recall (the share of relevant documents a search finds) and uptime. Executives measure throughput (work done per hour), cost, risk and customer experience. Your job is to convert one into the other.

The method is a chain: technical metric, then effect on a person's work, then effect on money or risk. For example, faster answers mean an agent handles more claims per hour, which means fewer overtime hours or a smaller backlog. Write each link down with a real number from the customer's own data.

Be honest about uncertainty. Use 'about' and give the assumption. An executive will forgive a rough estimate with a stated assumption. They will not forgive a precise-looking number that turns out to be invented.
subtopics.example: At the insurer, 40 claims agents work 7 productive hours a day. Before the fix, each claim took 12 minutes, partly spent waiting on the assistant. After the fix it takes 10 minutes. That is 5 claims per agent-hour rising to 6, a 20% uplift. At the same claim volume, the team saves about 47 agent-hours a day, worth roughly 2,100 pounds a day at a loaded cost of 45 pounds per hour.
subtopics.code:
# Turn a latency improvement into a business number
agents = 40
hours_per_day = 7
min_per_claim_before = 12.0
min_per_claim_after = 10.0      # measured after the latency fix
cost_per_hour_gbp = 45          # loaded cost of one agent-hour

rate_before = 60 / min_per_claim_before   # claims per agent-hour
rate_after = 60 / min_per_claim_after
uplift = rate_after / rate_before - 1

daily_claims = agents * hours_per_day * rate_before   # current volume
minutes_saved = daily_claims * (min_per_claim_before - min_per_claim_after)
hours_saved = minutes_saved / 60

print(f"Throughput uplift: {uplift:.0%}")                  # 20%
print(f"Agent-hours saved per day: {hours_saved:.0f}")     # 47
print(f"Value per day: GBP {hours_saved * cost_per_hour_gbp:,.0f}")

subtopics.title: Answer first: pyramid principle and SCQA
subtopics.body:
The pyramid principle, popularised by Barbara Minto, says to start with your main conclusion and then give the supporting points. Executives often read only the first two lines of a message, so those lines must carry the answer.

SCQA is a way to order the rest: Situation (what was happening), Complication (what went wrong), Question (what the reader wants to know) and Answer. In an incident update you usually put the Answer at the very top, then Situation, Complication, cause, prevention, and your ask.

Keep it to five to seven lines. Use plain words and numbers. End with one specific request, such as a 30-minute meeting with a named person, so the executive has something concrete to do.
subtopics.example: The CIO receives this at 13:50: 'Fixed at 13:40, no data lost.' The next lines explain that about 1,100 claims took three times longer between 10:00 and 13:40, that a vendor began rate limiting, that caching and an alert are now in place, and that you would like 30 minutes with their vendor manager. The CIO forwards it to the board unchanged, which is the sign of a good update.
subtopics.code:
ANSWER-FIRST UPDATE TEMPLATE
Answer:       <status in one line: fixed / workaround / still open>
Situation:    <what users were doing, when, which team>
Complication: <impact in business units: claims, patients, orders>
Cause:        <one sentence, or "under investigation, update at HH:MM">
Prevention:   <test, alert or change you have made or will make>
Ask:          <one decision or meeting you need, with a name>

Checks before sending:
[ ] First line makes sense if it is the only line read
[ ] No acronyms the reader would not use themselves
[ ] Every number has a unit and a time window

subtopics.title: Storytelling in reviews and presentations
subtopics.body:
Beyond incidents, you will present progress to executives in steering meetings and quarterly business reviews (QBRs), which are regular meetings where a vendor shows a customer the value delivered. The same answer-first rule applies at the level of a whole presentation.

A reliable structure has three parts. First, the result against the agreed success metric. Second, the story of how you got there, including one real user quote. Third, what comes next and the decision you need. Put the detail in an appendix so people can find it if they ask.

Rehearse the first 60 seconds. If the meeting is cut short, the executive should still leave knowing whether the project is working and what you need from them.
subtopics.example: For a retailer's demand forecasting pilot, your first slide says: 'Forecast error for fresh produce fell from 31% to 22% in 6 stores, cutting waste by an estimated 9 tonnes a month.' Slide two shows the store manager who now orders from the forecast. Slide three asks the COO to approve rollout to 40 more stores.
subtopics.code:
QBR OUTLINE (3 slides + appendix)
1. RESULT      Metric vs. target, baseline -> now, one sentence of impact
2. STORY       What changed for users; one quote; one chart
3. NEXT        Plan for next quarter; risks; THE DECISION WE NEED
Appendix       Method, data sources, detailed metrics, open issues

Rehearsal rule: say slide 1 aloud in under 60 seconds.

subtopics.title: Negotiating scope with trades
subtopics.body:
Negotiation in FDE work is mostly about scope: what gets built, by when, at what quality. A useful model is a triangle of scope, time and quality. If a customer adds scope, something else must move. Protect quality, because a buggy release damages trust more than a later one.

Anchor every conversation on the success metric agreed at the start. Ask: 'Does this new feature move the metric?' If it does, offer a trade, such as moving a lower-value item to phase 2. If it does not, put it on a backlog list that the sponsor has approved.

Let the executive sponsor choose between the options you present, and confirm their choice in writing. That way scope decisions are owned by the customer and cannot later turn into 'you promised'.
subtopics.example: Two weeks before go-live, a bank's operations head asks for three extra reports. You check each against the agreed metric (reduce manual reconciliation hours by 50%). One report helps the metric, two do not. You offer: add the useful report and move go-live by three days, or keep the date and deliver it in phase 2. The sponsor picks phase 2 and you confirm by email the same day.
subtopics.code:
Subject: Go-live scope - decision needed by Thursday

Hi Dana,

You asked for three new reports. Against our target (cut manual
reconciliation hours by 50%):

  - Branch summary, Audit export: do not affect the target

Options:

  B) Keep 14 Mar, deliver Exceptions report in phase 2 (by 4 Apr)
Branch summary and Audit export go on the phase 2 list either way.

glossary: CIO
Chief Information Officer, the executive responsible for a company's technology systems.
Escalation
When a problem is raised to a more senior person because the people handling it could not resolve it.
Incident
An event where a system stops working as users need, such as an outage or severe slowdown.
p95 latency
The response time that 95% of requests are faster than, a common way to describe slow-tail performance.
Workaround
A temporary fix that restores service while the real cause is investigated.
Root cause
The underlying reason a problem happened, as opposed to its visible symptom.
Pyramid principle
A writing method that states the main conclusion first and supporting points after.
SCQA
Situation, Complication, Question, Answer: a structure for ordering a short business story.
QBR
Quarterly business review, a regular meeting to show a customer the value delivered and agree next steps.
Executive sponsor
The senior customer leader who owns the project's success and makes final scope decisions.
practice: Take a technical result from a project you know (for example, 'query time dropped from 3s to 0.4s') and write the three-link chain from metric to user effect to business value, with your stated assumptions.
Rewrite a long status email you once sent (or a made-up one) into the six-line answer-first template. Ask a non-technical friend to read only the first line and tell you what happened.

Role-play a 10-minute escalation call with a friend playing an angry CIO whose dashboard is showing wrong numbers. Record it, then list every moment you explained technology before restating their impact.

moat.plain: Product judgment is deciding where a piece of work should live: in one customer's setup, or in the core product that every customer uses. A moat is a lasting advantage that makes it hard for competitors to take your customers, named after the water-filled ditch around a castle. In AI products, one of the strongest moats is proprietary process data: records of how real work gets done, such as the corrections users make, which you can use to improve your models. This concept is about making good 'build it where?' calls and turning deployments into that kind of advantage.
moat.analogy: A restaurant chef gets a request for a special dish. If one diner asks once, the chef makes it as a one-off without changing the menu. If many diners ask for it, it goes on the menu. Over the years the kitchen also learns which dishes people send back and why, and that knowledge is something a new restaurant across the street cannot copy.
moat.why: Every FDE hears 'can you just build this for us?' A logistics customer might want a special approval step for its EMEA team. If you fork the product for each such request, your company ends up maintaining dozens of slightly different versions, and the FDE team turns into an expensive consulting shop. If you route requests well, the field work becomes cheap product research and the product gets harder to compete with.

subtopics.title: The build-it-where decision
subtopics.body:
When a customer asks for something new, you have three places to put it. Configuration means settings the product already supports, such as a threshold or a list of approvers. An adapter is a small piece of code at the edge that connects the product to one customer's systems without changing the product itself. Core means the shared product code that every customer runs.

The default is configuration first, then an adapter, and core only with evidence. Evidence usually means two or more customers need something similar, and a general version fits where the product is heading.

Write down your reasoning each time. A short note ('config, because only Acme needs it; revisit if a second customer asks') makes it easy to spot repetition later.
subtopics.example: A freight company asks for invoices over 10,000 euros from its EMEA team to need a second approver. The product already supports approval rules, so this is configuration. A month later a retailer asks the same thing, and a third customer asks for approval chains by region. Now there is repetition, so you bring the product team a proposal for regional approval chains in core.
subtopics.code:
def where_should_it_live(req):
    """Rough triage for a customer request."""
    if req["supported_by_existing_settings"]:
        return "config"                     # no code change at all
    if req["customers_asking"] >= 2 and req["fits_roadmap"]:
        return "core (propose to product with evidence)"
    return "adapter (own it, test it, log it)"

requests = [
    {"name": "EMEA 2nd approver", "supported_by_existing_settings": True,
     "customers_asking": 1, "fits_roadmap": True},
    {"name": "Regional approval chains", "supported_by_existing_settings": False,
     "customers_asking": 3, "fits_roadmap": True},
    {"name": "Legacy AS/400 export", "supported_by_existing_settings": False,
     "customers_asking": 1, "fits_roadmap": False},
]
for r in requests:
    print(f"{r['name']:<26} -> {where_should_it_live(r)}")

subtopics.title: Isolating one-offs with config and adapters
subtopics.body:
Isolation means a customer-specific change cannot break anything else. Configuration does this naturally. Adapters do it by sitting between the customer's system and a clean interface the product already expects.

A good adapter has an owner (a named person), tests, and a record in a registry so people know it exists. Without those three things, adapters quietly become tech debt: code that costs more to maintain over time than it saved.

Never copy the core code into a customer branch to change one line. That is called forking, and it means every future product update has to be merged by hand into that customer's copy.
subtopics.example: A hospital exports patient appointments as a fixed-width text file instead of JSON. Rather than teaching the core scheduler to read that format, you write a 40-line adapter that converts the file into the standard appointment objects. The scheduler never knows the hospital is different.
subtopics.code:
# tenants/stmarys.yaml  - configuration, no code
tenant: stmarys
approvals:
  second_approver_over_eur: 10000
  approver_group: finance-emea
ingest:
  adapter: fixed_width_appointments   # registered adapter name
  owner: sam.k@vendor.example
  tests: tests/adapters/test_fixed_width.py

subtopics.title: The dark side: sprawl, crutches, bottlenecks
subtopics.body:
Custom-solution sprawl is what happens when one-off changes pile up without owners. Each deployment becomes unique, upgrades get slow, and new FDEs need weeks to understand an account.

Two related failure modes are common. An escalation crutch is when customers and internal teams send every problem to the FDE instead of using normal support, so the FDE stops building. A discovery bottleneck is when only one person understands an account, so everything waits for them.

The cure is visibility. Keep a registry of every customisation with its owner, tests and last change date, and review it monthly. Track how many tickets go to FDEs directly versus through support.
subtopics.example: Your team reviews its customisation registry and finds 14 adapters across 9 customers. Three have no owner because the engineer left, and two have no tests. You assign owners, add tests, and notice that four adapters all parse the same ERP export. That becomes a product proposal for a standard connector.
subtopics.code:
-- Find customisations that are turning into sprawl
SELECT customer,
       name,
       owner,
       has_tests,
       last_changed,
       CURRENT_DATE - last_changed AS days_since_change
FROM customisations
WHERE owner IS NULL
   OR has_tests = FALSE
   OR last_changed < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '180 days'
ORDER BY customer, name;

-- Spot repetition: the same source system handled more than once
SELECT source_system, COUNT(DISTINCT customer) AS customers
FROM customisations
GROUP BY source_system
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT customer) >= 2;

subtopics.title: R&D versus COGS
subtopics.body:
COGS (cost of goods sold) is the cost of delivering the product to a specific customer, such as hosting and people time spent on that account. R&D (research and development) is spending that improves the product for everyone. Investors and finance teams treat them very differently.

Bespoke FDE work for one customer is COGS. It lowers gross margin, which is revenue minus COGS, divided by revenue. Work that becomes a shared feature is closer to R&D, because it benefits every future customer.

This is why FDE organisations describe themselves as an R&D engine. Field work is paid discovery: the customer pays while you learn what the product should do. The trade only works if the learning actually flows back into the product.
subtopics.example: A customer pays 400,000 dollars a year. Hosting costs 60,000 and FDE time spent on bespoke work costs 180,000, so gross margin is 40%. In year two, half the bespoke work has become product features, FDE cost on the account drops to 90,000, and margin rises to about 62%. The next customer gets those features with no bespoke cost at all.
subtopics.code:
def gross_margin(revenue, hosting, fde_bespoke_cost):
    cogs = hosting + fde_bespoke_cost
    return (revenue - cogs) / revenue

revenue = 400_000
year1 = gross_margin(revenue, hosting=60_000, fde_bespoke_cost=180_000)
year2 = gross_margin(revenue, hosting=60_000, fde_bespoke_cost=90_000)

print(f"Year 1 gross margin: {year1:.0%}")   # 40%
print(f"Year 2 gross margin: {year2:.0%}")   # 62%
# The 90k of work moved into the product is now R&D:
# every future customer benefits without paying for it again.

subtopics.title: Process data as a moat
subtopics.body:
Features are easy to copy. A competitor can watch a demo and build something similar in months. What they cannot copy is data they do not have.

Process data is the record of how work actually happens inside customers: which suggestions users accepted, which they corrected, what the correct answer turned out to be, and which exceptions came up. It is created as a side effect of people using your product in real workflows.

To make it useful, capture it deliberately. Log each model suggestion together with what the user did and the final outcome, in a consistent format. Respect the contract: customers must agree to how their data is used, often in anonymised or aggregated form.
subtopics.example: An insurance claims product suggests a damage category for each claim. When an adjuster changes 'minor collision' to 'total loss', the product logs the original suggestion, the correction, and the final payout. After a year across 12 insurers, the vendor has hundreds of thousands of expert-labelled corrections that no new entrant can buy.

subtopics.title: The MLOps feedback loop
subtopics.body:
MLOps (machine learning operations) is the set of practices for training, evaluating, deploying and monitoring models in production. The feedback loop connects process data to better models: collect corrections, turn them into labelled training data, retrain, evaluate against a fixed test set, and deploy only if the new model is better.

The evaluation gate is the important part. A fixed holdout set (examples never used for training) lets you compare old and new models fairly. Without it, a retrain can make things worse and nobody notices.

Each turn of the loop makes the product better for every customer, which attracts more customers, which creates more data. That self-reinforcing cycle is the moat.
subtopics.example: Each month the claims vendor retrains its damage classifier on new corrections. In March the candidate model scores 0.89 accuracy on the holdout set against the current 0.86, with no drop on any insurer's subset, so it is promoted. In April the candidate scores lower on motorcycle claims, so it is held back and the team investigates.

glossary: Configuration
Settings the product already supports, changed without writing new code.
Adapter
A small piece of code at the edge that converts one customer's system into the interface the product expects.
Fork
A copy of the codebase changed for one customer, which then has to be kept in sync by hand.
Tech debt
Shortcuts in code that make future changes slower or riskier until they are cleaned up.
Custom-solution sprawl
The build-up of unowned, one-off customer changes that make every deployment unique.
Escalation crutch
When every problem is routed to the FDE instead of the product or support team.
COGS
Cost of goods sold: the cost of delivering the product to a specific customer.
Gross margin
Revenue minus COGS, divided by revenue; how much of each dollar is left after delivery costs.
Process data
Records of how real work happens in the product, such as user corrections and outcomes.
MLOps
Practices for training, evaluating, deploying and monitoring machine learning models in production.
practice: List five feature requests you have heard (from work, school projects or a product you use). Classify each as config, adapter or core using the triage function, and write one sentence of reasoning for each.
Design a customisation registry table (columns, types) and write the SQL to find entries with no owner and source systems handled for two or more customers. Load 10 fake rows and run it.

Pick a product you know (for example, an email spam filter). Write a one-page note describing what process data it could capture, what event schema you would log, and the promotion gate you would use before shipping a retrained model.

arc.plain: The engagement arc is the standard shape of an FDE project with one customer, from first meeting to handover. The course uses a 12-week, four-phase version: scope (weeks 1-2), prototype (weeks 3-6), harden (weeks 7-10) and hand over (weeks 11-12). Each phase has a clear output, such as agreed success criteria at the end of scoping or a trained customer team at the end of handover. Following the arc keeps a project from drifting and gives everyone a shared calendar.
arc.analogy: It is like renovating a kitchen. First you measure the room and agree what 'done' looks like. Then you mock up the layout with the family who will cook there. Then the electrician and plumber make it safe and up to code. Finally you hand over the keys, the warranty papers and a note on how the new oven works.
arc.why: Customers buy outcomes on a deadline. An FDE sent to a regional insurer that wants 'AI for claims' needs a plan that turns that vague wish into a measured result in about a quarter. Without the arc, projects stay stuck as demos that never go live, or they go live with nobody on the customer side able to run them.

subtopics.title: Weeks 1-2: find the pain and the baseline
subtopics.body:
Scoping starts with discovery: interviewing the people who do the work and the leaders who pay for it. You map the workflow step by step, note which systems hold the data, and learn who makes decisions.

The most important output of discovery is a baseline, which is a measured number describing how things work today. Without a baseline you cannot prove improvement later. Get it from the customer's own systems where possible, because they will trust their own data.

Start data access requests on day one. In large companies, getting access to a database can take weeks, and it often becomes the critical path (the chain of tasks that sets the earliest finish date).
subtopics.example: At a motor insurer, handlers say triage is slow. You pull timestamps from the claims system and find the median time from 'claim received' to 'claim triaged' is 4.1 hours over the last 90 days, and 6.8 hours on Mondays. That number becomes the baseline for the whole engagement.
subtopics.code:
-- Baseline: median and p90 time to triage, last 90 days (PostgreSQL)
SELECT
  team,
  COUNT(*) AS claims,
  percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (
    ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM triaged_at - received_at) / 3600
  ) AS median_hours,
  percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (
    ORDER BY EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM triaged_at - received_at) / 3600
  ) AS p90_hours
FROM claims
WHERE received_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'
  AND triaged_at IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY team
ORDER BY median_hours DESC;

subtopics.title: SMART criteria and choosing one pilot
subtopics.body:
SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. A SMART success criterion names the team, the metric, the baseline, the target, the deadline and where the number comes from.

Choose one pilot, meaning one workflow and one team, and keep it narrow. A good pilot has high value, available data, a willing user group and a clear metric. Score candidates on these and discuss the scores with the sponsor.

Also write down non-goals: things you will deliberately not do in this engagement. Non-goals are the easiest way to push back on scope creep later, because everyone already agreed to them.
subtopics.example: You compare three pilot options at the insurer. Motor claims triage scores highest because data is clean and the team lead is keen. Home claims fraud detection is valuable, but labels are poor. You agree: 'Reduce median triage time for the motor team from 4.1 hours to 1 hour by the end of week 10, measured from claims system timestamps.'
subtopics.code:
# Score candidate pilots with the sponsor (1 = poor, 5 = strong)
candidates = {
    "Motor triage":        {"value": 4, "data": 5, "users": 5, "metric": 5},
    "Home fraud detection": {"value": 5, "data": 2, "users": 3, "metric": 3},
    "Broker email routing": {"value": 3, "data": 4, "users": 3, "metric": 4},
}
weights = {"value": 0.35, "data": 0.25, "users": 0.2, "metric": 0.2}

for name, s in sorted(candidates.items(),
                      key=lambda kv: -sum(kv[1][k] * w for k, w in weights.items())):
    score = sum(s[k] * w for k, w in weights.items())
    print(f"{name:<22} {score:.2f}")

SMART = ("Reduce median motor-claim triage time from 4.1h to 1h "
         "by end of week 10, measured from claims system timestamps.")
NON_GOALS = ["Home claims", "Fraud scoring", "Changes to the payments system"]

subtopics.title: Weeks 3-6: prototype with users
subtopics.body:
Rapid prototyping means building a working version quickly and improving it through frequent feedback. Speed matters more than elegance here, because you are still learning what users need.

Work beside the end users, on real data. Sit with a claims handler while they use the prototype. Demo at least weekly, and keep a feedback log with each request, who asked, and what you decided.

Use real data from the start. Fake data hides the problems that matter most, such as messy fields and edge cases, and a demo on fake data will not convince the customer.
subtopics.example: In week 3 you ship a simple screen that suggests a triage category for each new motor claim. Handlers ignore it because it hides the policy number. In week 4 you add the policy number and a one-line reason. By week 6, handlers accept 70% of suggestions and triage time in the pilot group is already down to about 2 hours.

subtopics.title: Weeks 7-10: harden for production
subtopics.body:
Hardening turns a prototype into something people can depend on. It covers error handling (what happens when a call fails), logging (recording what happened for later debugging), data-quality checks, latency and caching, security review, and SLAs (service level agreements, the promised uptime and response times).

A common pattern is to wrap every call to an external system with retries and a timeout, log each attempt in a structured format, and check incoming data before using it. Bad data should be rejected loudly at the edge instead of producing wrong answers quietly.

Also agree who is on call, meaning who gets woken up if something breaks, and write that into a runbook (a step-by-step guide for operating and fixing the system).
subtopics.example: During hardening you find that the policy lookup service times out about once per 500 calls, and that 2% of claims arrive with an empty vehicle registration. You add three retries with exponential backoff and route claims with a missing registration to a manual queue. Both show up as counts on the monitoring dashboard.

subtopics.title: Measure against the criteria
subtopics.body:
At the end of hardening, measure the result the same way you measured the baseline: same query, same data source, same definition. Changing the definition midway makes the comparison meaningless and the customer will notice.

Report the number, the comparison to the target, and anything that affected it, such as a holiday week or a system outage. If you missed the target, say so plainly and explain what you learned. A clear miss with a credible plan is better than a fuzzy success.

This measured result is the evidence your account team uses to renew and expand the contract.
subtopics.example: Using the week-1 query restricted to the pilot team and weeks 9-10, the median motor triage time is 0.9 hours against a 4.1-hour baseline and a 1-hour target. The p90 dropped from 9.5 to 3.2 hours. You present both numbers to the sponsor along with the list of claims still handled manually.
subtopics.code:
-- Same definition as the baseline, before vs. after
WITH t AS (
  SELECT
    CASE WHEN received_at < DATE '2026-01-05' THEN 'baseline'
         WHEN received_at >= DATE '2026-03-02' THEN 'pilot_wk9_10'
    END AS period,
    EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM triaged_at - received_at) / 3600 AS hours
  FROM claims
  WHERE team = 'motor' AND triaged_at IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT period,
       COUNT(*) AS claims,
       percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY hours) AS median_hours,
       percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY hours) AS p90_hours
FROM t
WHERE period IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY period;

subtopics.title: Weeks 11-12: handover and a client CoE
subtopics.body:
Handover means the customer can run, fix and extend the system without you. The course calls the receiving team a client Center of Excellence (CoE): a small group of trained owners inside the customer who become the local experts.

A handover package includes documentation, a runbook, access and credentials transferred to customer owners, a training session with a recorded walkthrough, and a support path for the first few weeks.

Finally, write up what you learned for your own product team. Which parts did you have to build that the product should have had? This is the discovery half of the dual-value loop: delivery for the customer, and discovery for your company.
subtopics.example: In week 11 you train two engineers and one claims lead at the insurer. They run the weekly retraining themselves while you watch, then fix a staged failure using the runbook. In week 12 you hand over on-call and send your product team a note: three other customers will need the same policy-lookup connector.

glossary: Engagement

Pilot

Non-goals

practice: Pick a process you know (a library's book returns, a clinic's appointment booking). Write the baseline metric, how you would measure it, one SMART success criterion and three non-goals.
Build a 12-week plan in a spreadsheet for a made-up retailer pilot, with one row per week, the phase, the main deliverable and the customer people involved. Mark the critical path items.
Take a small script you have written that calls an external API. Harden it: add retries with backoff, a timeout, structured logging and one data-quality check, then write a half-page runbook for it.

pod.plain: A pod is the small team that runs an FDE engagement. In the course's model, a pod has one Echo, a Deployment Strategist who owns the customer relationship and scoping, and two Deltas, the forward deployed engineers who write the code. Leadership tells the pod what outcome to achieve and why it matters, and the pod decides how. Success is measured by time-to-value (TTV), the time from signing a contract to the customer getting measurable value.
pod.analogy: Think of a small film crew sent to shoot a documentary abroad. The producer handles permits, schedules and the relationship with local contacts. The two camera operators focus on filming. The studio back home says what story to tell and why, and trusts the crew on location to decide which shots to take.
pod.why: FDE work happens far from headquarters, in conditions that change weekly. A pod at a logistics company may find on day three that the data it planned to use does not exist. If every technical decision needed central approval, the pod would stall, and if engineers spent half their week in status meetings, nothing would ship. The pod model is designed to avoid both problems.

subtopics.title: Pod anatomy: one Echo, two Deltas
subtopics.body:
The Echo is the Deployment Strategist. They own the customer relationship, run scoping, manage stakeholders, write status reports, chase access requests and handle contracts and scheduling. They are technical enough to understand trade-offs but spend most of their time with people.

The Deltas are the engineers. They build, integrate, debug and deploy. Two engineers give the pod enough capacity to build and cover for each other, while staying small enough that coordination is cheap.

A clear split of responsibilities avoids confusion. A RACI chart is a simple tool for this: for each activity it names who is Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the outcome), Consulted and Informed.
subtopics.example: A pod starts at a national grocery chain. The Echo, Maya, runs the weekly steering meeting with the supply chain director and handles the security questionnaire. The Deltas, Ravi and Jo, build the demand forecast pipeline. When the director asks for a new report, Maya takes the request, checks it against the success metric and decides with the sponsor before it reaches the engineers.
subtopics.code:
# RACI for one pod (R = does it, A = owns outcome, C = consulted, I = informed)
activity:                 echo   delta_1  delta_2  customer_sponsor
  scoping_and_metrics:     A,R     C        C        C
  stakeholder_updates:     A,R     I        I        I
  access_and_security:     A,R     C        C        C
  data_pipeline:           I       A,R      R        I
  model_and_app:           I       R        A,R      I
  weekly_user_demo:        A       R        R        C
  scope_changes:           R       C        C        A

subtopics.title: Mission-type tactics (Auftragstaktik)
subtopics.body:
Auftragstaktik is a German term usually translated as mission-type tactics or mission command. It comes from 19th-century Prussian military doctrine. Commanders state the objective and the reason for it, and subordinates choose how to achieve it based on what they see on the ground.

In FDE terms, leadership writes an intent: the outcome, why it matters, the constraints (budget, security rules, deadlines) and what done looks like. Inside those limits, the pod picks the architecture, tools and order of work without central sign-off.

This only works if the intent is clear and the constraints are real. A vague intent leads to pods building the wrong thing. Too many constraints bring back central control by another name.
subtopics.example: Leadership's intent for a hospital pod: 'Cut outpatient no-shows at the two pilot clinics by a quarter within 12 weeks, because each no-show wastes a paid clinical slot. Constraints: patient data stays in the hospital's cloud tenant, and no changes to the booking system itself.' The pod chooses to build SMS reminders with a simple risk model, without asking headquarters to approve the design.
subtopics.code:
INTENT STATEMENT (leadership -> pod)
Objective:   Cut outpatient no-shows at Clinics A and B by 25%
Why:         Each no-show wastes a paid clinical slot and delays care
End state:   Hospital staff run the reminder process themselves
Constraints: - Patient data stays in the hospital cloud tenant
             - No changes to the booking system
             - Budget: 1 pod, 12 weeks
Decided by pod (no sign-off needed):
             architecture, model choice, order of work, tooling
Escalate to leadership only if:
             a constraint blocks the objective

subtopics.title: Protecting engineers from admin drag
subtopics.body:
Admin drag is the time engineers lose to non-engineering work: status meetings, access tickets, reporting, travel logistics and chasing approvals. The course cites estimates that this can take 40 to 60% of an engineer's time when nobody protects them.

The Echo's job is to absorb as much of this as possible. They attend the steering meetings, write the reports and chase the tickets, so the Deltas get long blocks of focused time.

Measure it instead of guessing. A quick look at calendars and ticket queues shows how much time goes to building versus everything else. If the build share is falling, fix it before it hurts delivery.
subtopics.example: In week 2 at the grocery chain, Ravi's calendar shows 18 hours of meetings out of 40, plus about 4 hours chasing database access. That is 55% admin. Maya takes over two recurring meetings and the access tickets, and in week 4 Ravi's admin share is down to about 20%.
subtopics.code:
# Estimate admin share from a calendar export (CSV: title,hours)
import csv

ADMIN_WORDS = ("status", "sync", "steering", "access", "report", "travel")

def admin_share(path, week_hours=40):
    admin = 0.0
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            if any(w in row["title"].lower() for w in ADMIN_WORDS):
                admin += float(row["hours"])
    return admin / week_hours

share = admin_share("ravi_week2.csv")
print(f"Admin share: {share:.0%}")
if share > 0.3:
    print("Action: Echo takes over recurring meetings and access chasing")

subtopics.title: Darwinistic adoption: ship small, keep what lives
subtopics.body:
Darwinistic adoption is the course's name for letting users decide which features survive. The pod ships small features quickly to real users, measures who uses them, keeps the ones that get adopted and removes the rest.

This replaces a big up-front roadmap inside the account. Instead of predicting what users want, you observe it. It requires instrumentation, meaning the product logs events like 'feature opened' or 'suggestion accepted' so you can count usage.

Set a rule before shipping, such as 'kill it if fewer than 20% of eligible users try it twice within three weeks'. Deciding the threshold in advance stops the team from keeping pet features alive.
subtopics.example: At the grocery chain the pod ships three features in two weeks: a forecast chart, a suggested order quantity and an email alert for likely stockouts. After three weeks, 78% of store managers use suggested orders weekly, 41% open the chart and 6% open the email. The email is removed and suggested orders get the next round of work.
subtopics.code:
-- Weekly adoption per feature over the last 3 weeks
WITH eligible AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM users WHERE role = 'store_manager'
),
active AS (
  SELECT feature, user_id
  FROM (
    SELECT feature, user_id, date_trunc('week', ts) AS wk
    FROM events
    WHERE ts >= now() - INTERVAL '21 days'
    GROUP BY feature, user_id, date_trunc('week', ts)
  ) w
  GROUP BY feature, user_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2          -- used in at least 2 of the 3 weeks
)
SELECT feature,
       COUNT(*)::float / (SELECT n FROM eligible) AS adoption,
       CASE WHEN COUNT(*)::float / (SELECT n FROM eligible) < 0.2
            THEN 'remove' ELSE 'keep' END AS decision
FROM active
GROUP BY feature
ORDER BY adoption DESC;

subtopics.title: Time-to-value and supporting metrics
subtopics.body:
Time-to-value (TTV) is the number of days from contract signature to the first moment the customer gets measurable value, for example the first week the pilot team hits its target. It is the pod's headline metric because it captures both speed and real impact.

The course lists supporting metrics from its Blueprint deck. Usage uplift is the growth in usage over time. Adoption depth is how many different features or workflows a customer relies on. Revenue protection is revenue at risk (such as an unhappy renewal) that the pod helped keep.

Define the value milestone before the engagement starts. If 'value' is defined after the fact, TTV becomes whatever makes the team look good.
subtopics.example: The grocery contract is signed on 6 January. The agreed value milestone is 'pilot stores reduce fresh produce waste by 10% for two consecutive weeks'. That happens in the week ending 30 March, so TTV is 83 days. Weekly active managers grew from 12 in February to 31 in March, a usage uplift of about 158%.
subtopics.code:
from datetime import date

contract_signed = date(2026, 1, 6)
value_milestone_hit = date(2026, 3, 30)   # agreed definition, set in week 1
ttv_days = (value_milestone_hit - contract_signed).days
print(f"Time-to-value: {ttv_days} days")                 # 83

wau_feb, wau_mar = 12, 31                                # weekly active managers
print(f"Usage uplift: {wau_mar / wau_feb - 1:.0%}")      # 158%

features_used = {"suggested_orders", "forecast_chart", "waste_report"}
features_available = 5
print(f"Adoption depth: {len(features_used)}/{features_available} features")

lastmile.plain: Last-mile onboarding is the work of getting a product that already works in demos to work inside one specific customer's messy environment. The name borrows from delivery companies, where the final stretch to the customer's door is often the hardest and most expensive part. Onboarding typically stalls on three things: undocumented APIs (interfaces with no reliable description), broken schemas (data structures that do not match what the product expects) and workflow exceptions (special cases in how the customer works). FDEs fix these in real time and capture each fix so the next customer is faster.
lastmile.analogy: Moving into a new flat with furniture that fit perfectly in the showroom. On moving day, the stairwell is narrow, one wall is not straight, and the building has a rule about when you can use the lift. Someone has to measure, adjust and work around each problem, and a good mover writes down the tricks for the next job in the same building.
lastmile.why: The sale assumed clean integrations, but real customers run old systems with no documentation, data that means different things in different regions, and rules like 'claims over 50,000 pounds go to Jane'. The customer's R&D team is usually too busy to help. If onboarding stalls, the customer never reaches value and the renewal is at risk, so this is where FDEs earn their keep.

subtopics.title: Why onboarding stalls: the delivery gap
subtopics.body:
The delivery gap is the distance between what the product does in a clean demo and what it must do inside a real customer. The course's Blueprint deck names three causes: AI complexity, messy data and stretched R&D teams.

In practice, most blockers fall into the three buckets above: APIs, schemas and exceptions. A useful first step is an integration inventory, a list of every system the product must talk to, with how it connects, who owns it, and what is known about it.

The inventory turns an overwhelming 'nothing works' into a list of specific problems, each with an owner and a next step. It also shows which problems you have seen before at other customers.
subtopics.example: At a regional insurer, onboarding the claims assistant touches five systems. The inventory shows the policy database is fine, the document store has an API with no docs, the claims system exports CSVs where the 'status' column means different things in two regions, and there are three unwritten routing rules. Now there are four concrete work items instead of one vague delay.

INTEGRATION INVENTORY - Northshire Insurance
system          connects via      owner          docs?   known issues            status
policy_db       Postgres read     IT (K. Lowe)   yes     none                    DONE
doc_store       REST API          vendor, legacy NO      auth unclear, paging?   PROBE
claims_export   nightly CSV (S3)  Claims ops     partial 'status' differs N/S    REPAIR
routing_rules   people's heads    Claims leads   NO      >50k to Jane, fraud flag ENCODE
sso             SAML              IT security    yes     group names TBC         WAITING
# Every row gets an owner and a next action before the weekly sync.

subtopics.title: Probing an undocumented API
subtopics.body:
When an API has no documentation, you learn it by observation. Ask for a sandbox (a test copy of the system) or permission to read-only call production. Watch real traffic if another application already uses it.

Make small, careful requests and save every response to a file. These saved responses are called fixtures. They show the real field names, types, pagination (how results are split across pages) and error formats.

Write down what you learn as you go, including surprises, and confirm unclear points with the customer's engineers. Your notes become the documentation that did not exist.
subtopics.example: The insurer's document store has a /documents endpoint and nobody knows its parameters. You call it with a test claim ID, find the results come 50 at a time with a next_cursor field, discover that dates are strings in day/month/year order, and see it returns HTTP 200 with an error field instead of a proper error code when a claim is missing. Each finding goes into your notes and fixtures.
subtopics.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Probe an undocumented API and save responses as fixtures
set -euo pipefail
BASE="https://docstore.sandbox.northshire.example/api"
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer ${DOCSTORE_TOKEN}"
mkdir -p fixtures

# 1. Normal request
curl -sS -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/documents?claim_id=C-10442" \
  | tee fixtures/documents_ok.json | jq 'keys'

# 2. Follow pagination: which field holds the next page?
jq -r '.next_cursor // "none"' fixtures/documents_ok.json

# 3. A claim that does not exist: what does an error look like?
curl -sS -o fixtures/documents_missing.json -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n" \
  -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/documents?claim_id=DOES-NOT-EXIST"
jq '.' fixtures/documents_missing.json

subtopics.title: A typed wrapper with retries and tests
subtopics.body:
A wrapper is a small module that hides a messy API behind a clean, predictable interface. The product calls the wrapper, and only the wrapper knows about the API's quirks.

Typed means the wrapper returns well-defined objects with checked fields. In Python, Pydantic models do this: they validate incoming data and convert types, so a date string becomes a real date. Add retries for temporary failures and turn the API's odd error format into a normal exception.

Test the wrapper against the fixtures you saved. Those tests keep working even when the sandbox is down, and they catch it if someone changes the parsing logic by mistake.
subtopics.example: Your wrapper for the insurer's document store follows the cursor to collect all pages, converts '14/03/2026' into a date, and raises DocumentNotFound when the body contains an error field. The claims assistant now just calls list_documents('C-10442') and gets a clean list.

subtopics.title: Repairing broken schemas at the boundary
subtopics.body:
A schema is the expected structure of data: which columns exist, their types, and what values mean. Broken schemas include columns that mean different things by region, nulls (missing values) in key fields, and types that drift, such as a number column that sometimes contains text.

Repair data at the boundary, the point where it enters your system. Map codes to one shared meaning, convert types, and validate. Rows that cannot be repaired go to a quarantine table with a reason, so nothing is silently dropped.

Keep the mapping rules in a readable table that the customer can review. They know what their codes mean better than you do.
subtopics.example: In the insurer's claims export, status 'C' means 'closed' in the North region and 'contested' in the South. Some rows have a blank claim_id and some amounts contain '1,250.00' as text. You map status by region, convert amounts, and quarantine the 0.4% of rows with no claim_id for the claims ops team to review.
subtopics.code:
import pandas as pd

STATUS_MAP = {                          # reviewed with Claims ops
    ("North", "C"): "closed",
    ("South", "C"): "contested",
    ("North", "O"): "open", ("South", "O"): "open",
}

def repair(df: pd.DataFrame) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    df = df.copy()
    df["status"] = [STATUS_MAP.get((r, s), "unknown")
                    for r, s in zip(df["region"], df["status"])]
    df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(
        df["amount"].astype(str).str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")

    bad = df["claim_id"].isna() | df["amount"].isna() | (df["status"] == "unknown")
    quarantine = df[bad].assign(reason="missing id, bad amount or unknown status")
    return df[~bad], quarantine

clean, quarantine = repair(pd.read_csv("claims_export.csv"))
print(len(clean), "clean rows;", len(quarantine), "quarantined")

subtopics.title: Encoding workflow exceptions as rules
subtopics.body:
Workflow exceptions are special cases in how a customer does its work, such as 'claims over 50,000 pounds go to Jane' or 'anything flagged for fraud skips the fast track'. They are often unwritten and only discovered when users say 'that is wrong'.

Encode them as data-driven rules in the pipeline, kept in a configuration file that is separate from product code. Each rule has a condition and an action. The product reads the rules; it does not contain them.

Order matters, so evaluate rules top to bottom and stop at the first match. Keep a test case for every rule, taken from a real example the users gave you.
subtopics.example: Claims leads at the insurer tell you three rules: claims over 50,000 pounds go to the senior handler, anything with a fraud flag goes to the investigations queue, and glass-only claims are auto-approved under 500 pounds. You put these in a YAML file and the router picks them up without any change to the claims assistant.
subtopics.code:
import yaml

RULES_YAML = """
- name: fraud_first
  when: {fraud_flag: true}
  route: investigations
- name: large_claims
  when: {amount_gt: 50000}
  route: senior_handler_jane
- name: glass_fast_track
  when: {claim_type: glass, amount_lt: 500}
  route: auto_approve
"""
RULES = yaml.safe_load(RULES_YAML)

def matches(claim, cond):
    if "fraud_flag" in cond and claim.get("fraud_flag") != cond["fraud_flag"]: return False
    if "claim_type" in cond and claim.get("claim_type") != cond["claim_type"]: return False
    if "amount_gt" in cond and not claim["amount"] > cond["amount_gt"]: return False
    if "amount_lt" in cond and not claim["amount"] < cond["amount_lt"]: return False
    return True

def route(claim):
    for rule in RULES:                         # first match wins
        if matches(claim, rule["when"]):
            return rule["route"]
    return "standard_queue"

print(route({"amount": 72000, "fraud_flag": False, "claim_type": "motor"}))

subtopics.title: Playbooks, portals and PSA automation
subtopics.body:
Each fix is only valuable once if you throw it away. A playbook is a reusable onboarding plan made of templates: task lists, connector code, mapping tables and rules that worked before. A dynamic playbook adapts to the customer, for example adding the document-store tasks only if the customer uses that system.

PSA stands for professional services automation: software for running client projects, including plans, resourcing and time tracking. Tools in this space, such as Rocketlane, which focuses on customer onboarding, offer shared workspaces, reusable project templates, client-facing portals and AI features that help draft plans and updates.

A client portal gives the customer a live view of plan, status and their own open tasks. That removes many status meetings and makes it obvious when a delay is waiting on the customer's side.
subtopics.example: After Northshire, your team saves the document-store wrapper, the regional status mapping and the routing rule template into the playbook. When a second insurer running the same document store signs, the plan starts with those tasks pre-filled and the wrapper already tested. Their integration takes 4 days instead of 3 weeks.

      - id: docstore

        include_if: "customer.systems contains 'docstore_legacy'"
        template: connectors/docstore_legacy/
        days: 2
      - {id: map, title: "Review status mapping with claims ops",
         owner: customer, template: mappings/claims_status.csv, days: 3}
      - {id: rules, title: "Capture routing exceptions",
         template: rules/claims_routing.yaml, days: 2}
portal:
  visible_to_customer: [plan, milestones, customer_tasks, blockers]
  weekly_update: auto_draft   # reviewed by Echo before sending

practice: Pick a free public API with thin documentation. Probe three endpoints with curl, save fixtures, and write a one-page 'what we learned' note covering fields, pagination and error format.

Create a messy CSV of 30 rows (mixed date formats, text in number columns, a code that means different things by region). Write a repair function that returns clean and quarantined rows, with a test for each problem.

Write a YAML onboarding playbook for a made-up SaaS product with two phases and at least one conditional task. Then write a short script that prints the task list for a customer given which systems they use.

interview.plain: An interview loop is the series of interviews a company runs before making an offer. FDE loops test more than coding puzzles. The course's blueprint weights four pillars: deep technical understanding (40%), practical implementation (30%), customer scenario and communication (20%) and business acumen (10%). Preparing well means spending your time roughly in proportion to those weights and having a portfolio and stories that prove each one.
interview.analogy: It is like a driving test that includes a theory exam, a practical drive, a section where you give directions to a lost tourist, and a few questions on the cost of running a car. Practising only parallel parking would leave you unprepared for most of it.
interview.why: Many engineers prepare only with LeetCode-style algorithm puzzles and then struggle when an FDE interviewer plays a vague customer or asks them to build against a real API in 90 minutes. Knowing what is scored lets you practise the right things, and it lets you show why an FDE role suits you instead of a standard software engineering role.

subtopics.title: How the loop is scored
subtopics.body:
Algorithm puzzles, often called DSA (data structures and algorithms) questions, are a small part of an FDE loop. Keep them warm with light practice, but most of the score comes from the four pillars.

A simple way to plan is to split your available prep hours by the pillar weights, then subtract what you are already strong at. Someone with a strong backend background might shift hours from implementation toward customer role-play.

Track your practice. After each mock interview, score yourself per pillar from 1 to 5 and write one improvement. Over a few weeks you will see which pillar is holding you back.
subtopics.example: You have 60 hours before your onsite. By weight that is 24 hours of technical depth, 18 of timed builds, 12 of customer role-play and 6 of business reading. Since you already build APIs daily, you move 6 build hours to customer role-play, which is your weakest area.
subtopics.code:
weights = {"deep_technical": 0.40, "implementation": 0.30,
           "customer": 0.20, "business": 0.10}
total_hours = 60

plan = {p: round(total_hours * w) for p, w in weights.items()}
print("By weight:", plan)          # 24 / 18 / 12 / 6

# Adjust for your own strengths and weaknesses
plan["implementation"] -= 6        # already strong: build APIs daily
plan["customer"] += 6              # weakest pillar in mock interviews
print("Adjusted:", plan)

mock_scores = {"deep_technical": 3, "implementation": 4, "customer": 2, "business": 3}
weakest = min(mock_scores, key=mock_scores.get)
print("Focus next mock on:", weakest)

subtopics.title: Deep technical: surviving follow-ups
subtopics.body:
The technical depth pillar checks whether you understand how the tools you use work underneath. Interviewers ask a question, then keep asking 'why' and 'what if' until they reach the edge of your knowledge.

A good way to prepare is a layered answer. Layer one is a one-sentence summary. Layer two is the mechanism. Layer three is failure modes and trade-offs. Layer four is a real example with numbers from your own work.

When you reach the limit of what you know, say so and reason out loud: 'I have not measured that, but I would expect X because Y, and I would check it by Z.' That scores better than bluffing.
subtopics.example: Asked 'Why does RAG sometimes give wrong answers?', you say it retrieves text and then generates from it. You explain chunking and embedding search, then list failure modes: the right chunk is never retrieved, the chunk is retrieved but ranked too low, or the model ignores it. You finish with how your own project's grounding check caught unsupported answers.
subtopics.code:
LAYERED ANSWER TEMPLATE  (practise for 10 core topics)
Topic: Why does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fail?
L1 Summary:   It answers from retrieved text; if retrieval or use of
              that text fails, the answer is wrong.
L2 Mechanism: chunk docs -> embed -> vector search -> top-k into prompt
L3 Failures:  (a) right chunk never retrieved (bad chunking/embedding)
              (b) retrieved but ranked low (needs hybrid search/rerank)
              (c) model ignores or contradicts context (needs grounding check)
              (d) stale index (needs refresh pipeline)
L4 Evidence:  "In my project, adding keyword search to vectors raised
              retrieval hit rate on my test set; grounding check flagged
              unsupported answers before users saw them."
If stuck:     "I have not measured that. I'd expect ... because ...
              I'd verify by ..."

subtopics.title: The practical build round
subtopics.body:
In the implementation round you usually get 60 to 90 minutes to build something small against a real API or dataset. Interviewers look for working code, sensible structure, handling of failure paths and clear talk about trade-offs.

A reliable approach: restate the task and ask two or three clarifying questions, get the simplest end-to-end version working, then add error handling and tests, then improve. Talk as you go, especially when you choose not to do something because of time.

Practise under a timer. Timed practice reveals the things that slow you down, such as setting up a project or remembering library syntax.
subtopics.example: The task: 'Given an orders API that pages results and sometimes returns 429, compute total revenue per customer.' You first write a loop that follows pages, then add a retry on 429, then write two tests with a fake client: one for pagination and one for a rate-limited page. You mention that for large data you would stream results instead of holding them all in memory.

subtopics.title: The customer scenario round
subtopics.body:
Here an interviewer role-plays a customer with a vague request, such as 'We want to use AI to improve our supply chain.' You are scored on discovery questions, scoping, and explaining trade-offs to someone who is not an engineer.

Resist the urge to propose a solution in the first five minutes. Ask about the business goal, who feels the pain, how it is measured today, what data exists, and who decides. Then summarise what you heard and propose a thin first slice with a metric.

When you explain trade-offs, use the customer's words. Say 'faster answers but slightly more wrong ones' instead of 'lower precision at higher recall'.
subtopics.example: The interviewer, playing a logistics director, says late deliveries are hurting them. You ask what 'late' means, how often it happens, and where the delay starts. You learn 14% of deliveries miss their window and most delays start at the depot. You propose a 6-week pilot at one depot predicting which loads will miss their window, measured against that 14%.
subtopics.code:
CUSTOMER ROUND: DISCOVERY CHECKLIST
Goal      "What would success look like in six months?"
Pain      "Who feels this most? Can you walk me through a bad day?"
Baseline  "How do you measure it today? What is the number?"
Data      "Where does that data live? Who owns it? How fresh is it?"
Decision  "Who signs off? Who could block this?"
Limits    "Budget, deadlines, compliance rules I should know about?"
---
Summarise: "So the core problem is ___, measured by ___, currently ___."
Propose:   "A ___-week pilot on ___, aiming to move ___ from ___ to ___."
Trade-off: explain in their terms (time, cost, risk, customer impact)

subtopics.title: Business acumen: the numbers FDE leaders watch
subtopics.body:
The business pillar checks that you understand why a company funds FDEs. The key terms are NRR, TTV, margin-for-moat and custom sprawl.

NRR (net revenue retention) measures how much revenue you keep and grow from existing customers over a year, including expansions and after losses. Above 100% means existing customers are spending more than a year ago. FDE work aims to raise it by making customers successful enough to expand.

Margin-for-moat is the idea of accepting lower early margins on hands-on delivery in exchange for larger, stickier accounts and product learning. Custom sprawl is the risk that undoes it. Be ready to explain both with a short example.
subtopics.example: A company starts the year with 10 million dollars of annual recurring revenue (ARR) from existing customers. During the year those customers expand by 2.5 million, downgrade by 0.4 million and 0.6 million churns (cancels). NRR is (10 + 2.5 - 0.4 - 0.6) / 10 = 115%.
subtopics.code:
def nrr(start_arr, expansion, contraction, churn):
    """Net revenue retention for a cohort of existing customers."""
    return (start_arr + expansion - contraction - churn) / start_arr

value = nrr(start_arr=10_000_000, expansion=2_500_000,
            contraction=400_000, churn=600_000)
print(f"NRR: {value:.0%}")      # 115%

# Interview talking point: how an FDE moves each term
levers = {
    "expansion":   "measured pilot results unlock new teams and use cases",
    "contraction": "adoption work keeps seats and usage from shrinking",
    "churn":       "incident handling and TTV protect renewals",
}

subtopics.title: Portfolio, STAR stories and the offer
subtopics.body:
A portfolio is proof. The course suggests two projects: Project A, an agentic RAG service with a fine-tuned open model and evaluations, and Project B, a coding agent built with LangGraph. What makes them strong is measured results: faithfulness, latency, cost and the failures you fixed.

STAR stories are short answers to behavioural questions, structured as Situation, Task, Action, Result. Prepare one or two per pillar from your own work, such as Vukti, DATAVORE or your MCP projects. Use 'I' for what you did, and end with a number.

Before recruiter calls, research compensation for FDE roles at your target companies using public salary-sharing sites and people you know in the field. Negotiate on total compensation, which combines base salary, bonus and equity.
subtopics.example: For the customer pillar, you might prepare: Situation, a client's data pipeline kept failing overnight. Task, you owned making it reliable. Action, you interviewed the ops team, found a schema change upstream, and added validation and alerts. Result, failed nightly runs dropped from several a week to none over the following month, with the actual figures taken from your own logs.
