practice: Write layered answers (four layers) for three topics you claim to know well, then ask a friend to push with 'why' follow-ups for 10 minutes each. Note where you hit the edge.
Do one timed 75-minute build: pick a public paginated API, compute an aggregate, handle rate limits and write two tests. Afterwards write down what slowed you down.
Build a STAR story bank with at least one story per pillar from your own projects, each ending in a real number. Record yourself telling two of them and cut each to under two minutes.

projecta.plain: Project A is a portfolio project: an agentic RAG service. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means the system first searches a document collection for relevant passages and then asks a language model to answer using them. Agentic means the system can check its own work and choose what to do next, such as rewriting a weak search query and trying again. The project combines a vector database, a fine-tuned open model, an agent graph, an API and evaluations that report quality, speed and cost.
projecta.analogy: It is like a careful research librarian. They search the shelves, look at what they found, and if it does not answer the question they rephrase and search again. Before handing you an answer, they check that every claim is backed by a page they can point to, and they keep a log of how long each request took.
projecta.why: Enterprise customers ask FDEs for 'a chatbot over our documents' more than almost anything else, and the hard parts are exactly the ones this project covers: permissions, weak retrieval, hallucinations and cost. An FDE who can show a deployed service with real evaluation numbers, for example for an insurer's policy documents, has a concrete story for every interview pillar.

subtopics.title: The architecture at a glance
subtopics.body:
The service has five parts. A FastAPI endpoint receives questions. A LangGraph state machine controls the steps. PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension stores document chunks and their embeddings (lists of numbers that represent meaning). A generation model writes the answer. A metrics log records quality, latency and cost for every request.

Keeping everything in one Postgres database is a deliberate simplification. Pinecone or Milvus are dedicated vector databases that also work, but pgvector means one system to run and back up, and permissions can live next to the data.

Draw the architecture before writing code. Interviewers will ask you to walk through it, and a clear diagram also helps you decide what to build first.
subtopics.example: A mock scenario: an insurer wants staff to ask questions about 3,000 policy documents. Underwriters may see all documents; call-centre staff may only see customer-facing ones. The diagram shows where each of these requirements is handled: permissions in retrieval, citations in generation, and a grounding check before the answer is returned.
subtopics.code:
+-------------------+
 user  ---> |  FastAPI /ask     |  auth -> user groups
            +---------+---------+
                      v
            +-------------------+      +---------------------------+
            | LangGraph agent   | ---> | Postgres + pgvector        |
            | retrieve          |      | chunks, embeddings, ACLs   |
            | grade -> rewrite  | <--- | hybrid search (vec + text) |
            | generate          |      +---------------------------+
            | grounding check   | ---> generation model (QLoRA-tuned)
            +---------+---------+
                      v
            metrics log: faithfulness, latency_ms, tokens, cost

subtopics.title: Hybrid retrieval with permissions in pgvector
subtopics.body:
Documents are split into chunks of a few hundred words, each stored with its embedding and a list of groups allowed to see it. That list is an ACL (access control list).

Hybrid search combines vector similarity, which finds passages with similar meaning, and keyword search, which finds exact terms like policy codes that embeddings can miss. A common way to merge the two ranked lists is reciprocal rank fusion (RRF): each result scores 1 / (k + rank) in each list, and the scores are summed.

Apply the permission filter inside the search queries so a user can never retrieve a chunk they are not allowed to see, even indirectly through the model's answer.
subtopics.example: A call-centre agent asks 'Is flood damage covered under HX-200?' Vector search finds chunks about water damage in general. Keyword search finds the exact 'HX-200' schedule. RRF puts the HX-200 flood clause first. An underwriting-only annex is excluded because the agent's group is not in its ACL.
subtopics.code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id             bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  doc_id         text NOT NULL,
  allowed_groups text[] NOT NULL,                  -- ACL
  content        text NOT NULL,
  tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', content)) STORED,
  embedding      vector(1024)
);
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING gin (tsv);

-- $1 query embedding, $2 query text, $3 user's groups (text[])
WITH semantic AS (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS r
  FROM chunks WHERE allowed_groups && $3
  ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 20
), keyword AS (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv, q) DESC) AS r
  FROM chunks, plainto_tsquery('english', $2) AS q
  WHERE tsv @@ q AND allowed_groups && $3
  ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv, q) DESC LIMIT 20
)
SELECT c.id, c.doc_id, c.content, SUM(1.0 / (60 + s.r)) AS rrf_score
FROM (SELECT * FROM semantic UNION ALL SELECT * FROM keyword) s
JOIN chunks c USING (id)
GROUP BY c.id, c.doc_id, c.content
ORDER BY rrf_score DESC LIMIT 5;

subtopics.title: The agent graph in LangGraph
subtopics.body:
LangGraph lets you describe the agent as a graph: nodes are steps (functions), edges say what runs next, and a shared state dictionary carries data between steps. A conditional edge chooses the next node based on the state.

The key loop is retrieve, grade, and either generate or rewrite and retrieve again. Always cap the number of attempts. Without a cap, a question with no good answer in the documents can loop forever and burn tokens.

When attempts run out, the generate step should say it could not find support in the documents instead of guessing. That behaviour is often more valuable to an enterprise than a confident wrong answer.
subtopics.example: The question 'What is the excess for HX-200 flood claims?' first retrieves general flood text. The grader marks it not relevant. The rewrite step produces 'HX-200 policy schedule flood excess amount', the second retrieval finds the schedule table, the grader marks it relevant, and generation answers with a citation. Total attempts: 2.
subtopics.code:
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3

class RAGState(TypedDict, total=False):
    question: str
    query: str
    chunks: list[dict]
    relevant: bool
    attempts: int
    answer: str
    grounded: bool

# search, grade_chunks, rewrite_query, call_generator, grounding_check
# are your own functions (see the other subtopics).
def retrieve(s):  return {"chunks": search(s["query"]), "attempts": s["attempts"] + 1}
def grade(s):     return {"relevant": grade_chunks(s["question"], s["chunks"])}
def rewrite(s):   return {"query": rewrite_query(s["question"], s["query"])}
def generate(s):  return {"answer": call_generator(s["question"], s["chunks"], s["relevant"])}
def check(s):     return {"grounded": grounding_check(s["answer"], s["chunks"])}

def route(s):
    if s["relevant"] or s["attempts"] >= MAX_ATTEMPTS:   # retry cap
        return "generate"
    return "rewrite"

g = StateGraph(RAGState)
for name, fn in [("retrieve", retrieve), ("grade", grade), ("rewrite", rewrite),
                 ("generate", generate), ("check", check)]:
    g.add_node(name, fn)
g.add_edge(START, "retrieve")
g.add_edge("retrieve", "grade")
g.add_conditional_edges("grade", route, {"generate": "generate", "rewrite": "rewrite"})
g.add_edge("rewrite", "retrieve")
g.add_edge("generate", "check")
g.add_edge("check", END)
agent = g.compile()
# agent.invoke({"question": q, "query": q, "attempts": 0})

subtopics.title: Grading evidence with structured output
subtopics.body:
The grader is a small, cheap model call that answers one question: do these passages contain what is needed to answer? You want a yes or no you can branch on, so ask the model for structured output.

With the Anthropic Messages API, one reliable way is to define a tool with a JSON schema and force the model to call it using tool_choice. The tool is never actually executed; its input is simply the structured answer you read back.

The same pattern works for the grounding check: give the answer and the passages, and ask for a list of claims with a supported flag for each. Store the result so you can compute faithfulness later.
subtopics.example: For the HX-200 question with general flood passages, the grader returns relevant: false with the reason 'passages describe flood cover generally but do not mention HX-200 or an excess amount'. That reason is logged, which later helps you see that most retries come from product codes missing in embeddings.

subtopics.title: QLoRA fine-tuning the generator
subtopics.body:
Fine-tuning means training an existing model further on your own examples so it learns a style or format. Full fine-tuning of a large model needs a lot of GPU memory. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) trains only small added matrices instead of all the weights. QLoRA does the same on top of a model loaded in 4-bit precision, which cuts memory enough to fine-tune a 7 to 8 billion parameter model on a single large GPU.

The course suggests an open model such as Llama 3 or Mistral. Train it on a few thousand examples of the answer format you want, for example 'answer, then cited clause numbers'. Fine-tuning teaches format and tone; the facts should still come from retrieval.

Always compare the tuned model against the base model on the same evaluation set. If the tuned model is not measurably better on your metrics, use the base model and say so in your write-up.
subtopics.example: You build 2,000 question and answer pairs from policy documents, each answer ending with clause citations in the insurer's house style. After QLoRA training, the share of answers with correctly formatted citations on your test set rises well above the base model's, and you report the exact figures from your own run.
subtopics.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, prepare_model_for_kbit_training

BASE_MODEL = "BASE_MODEL"          # placeholder: an open Llama 3 or Mistral checkpoint

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,             # the "Q" in QLoRA
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL, quantization_config=bnb,
                                             device_map="auto")
model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)

lora = LoraConfig(
    r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"],   # attention layers
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)
model = get_peft_model(model, lora)
model.print_trainable_parameters()   # a small fraction of the total
# Next: train with transformers Trainer or TRL's SFTTrainer on your Q&A pairs,
# then save only the adapter: model.save_pretrained("adapters/policy-qa")

subtopics.title: Evaluation and serving: the numbers that matter
subtopics.body:
Evaluations turn a demo into evidence. Track three things per request. Faithfulness is the share of claims in the answer that are supported by the retrieved passages. Latency is time per request; report p95, the time 95% of requests beat. Token cost is input and output tokens multiplied by the model's prices.

Build a fixed evaluation set of 100 to 200 real-looking questions with expected source documents. Run it after every change, such as adding keyword search or the grader, and keep a table of results over time.

Serve the agent behind a FastAPI endpoint that times each request and logs the metrics. Package it with Docker so anyone can run it, and deploy it to show you can take it to production.
subtopics.example: Your results table might show that adding keyword search to vector search raised the share of questions whose correct document appeared in the top 5, and that the grader added some latency per retry. You report faithfulness, p95 latency and cost per 1,000 queries for each version, using the numbers your own runs produced.
subtopics.code:
import statistics, time
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()
PRICE_IN, PRICE_OUT = 0.0, 0.0      # fill in per-million-token prices for your model
LOG: list[dict] = []

class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str

@app.post("/ask")
def ask(req: Ask):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    out = agent.invoke({"question": req.question, "query": req.question, "attempts": 0})
    ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    LOG.append({"latency_ms": ms, "grounded": out["grounded"],
                "tok_in": out.get("tok_in", 0), "tok_out": out.get("tok_out", 0)})
    return {"answer": out["answer"], "grounded": out["grounded"], "latency_ms": round(ms)}

def report(log: list[dict]) -> dict:
    lat = [r["latency_ms"] for r in log]
    cost = sum(r["tok_in"] * PRICE_IN + r["tok_out"] * PRICE_OUT for r in log) / 1e6
    return {
        "faithfulness": sum(r["grounded"] for r in log) / len(log),
        "p95_ms": statistics.quantiles(lat, n=20)[18],   # 95th percentile
        "cost_per_1k_queries": cost / len(log) * 1000,
    }

glossary: RAG
Retrieval-augmented generation: search documents first, then have a model answer using what was found.
Agentic
Able to inspect intermediate results and choose the next step, such as retrying a search.
Embedding
A list of numbers representing the meaning of text, used to find similar passages.
pgvector
A PostgreSQL extension that stores embeddings and runs similarity search.
Hybrid search
Combining vector similarity search with keyword search to get better results.
ACL
Access control list: which users or groups may see a given item.
LangGraph
A library for building agents as graphs of steps that share a state.
QLoRA
Fine-tuning small adapter matrices on top of a model loaded in 4-bit precision to save memory.
Faithfulness
The share of an answer's claims that are supported by the retrieved sources.
p95 latency
The response time that 95% of requests are faster than.
practice: Load 50 documents of your choice into Postgres with pgvector, create the chunks table with an ACL column, and run the hybrid RRF query for five questions. Show that a user without the right group never sees restricted chunks.

Build the LangGraph agent with stub functions first (search returns fixed chunks, grader returns False twice then True). Confirm the retry cap works, then swap in real retrieval and the tool-based grader.

Create a 100-question evaluation set, run it against two versions of your service (vector-only vs. hybrid), and publish a results table with faithfulness, p95 latency and cost per 1,000 queries plus the biggest failure category you found.
